subtitle: Lesson 28 · Other Landmark Quantum Algorithms

eyebrow: What you actually get out of it

steps.label: A: N×N, Hermitian, sparse; b: a known vector
Output is NOT x printed as N classical numbers
steps.sub: It's a quantum state |x⟩ with amplitudes proportional to x's entries

steps.label: A quantum encoding, not a readable result
steps.sub: Whether that's useful depends entirely on what you need next

steps.label: Headline: O(log N · s² · κ² / ε) vs. classical O(N·s·κ)
steps.sub: On dimension N alone, the advantage looks exponential

eyebrow: Three caveats that overturn the headline
code:
1. State prep: loading b can itself cost O(N)
   -> cancels the log(N) advantage before the algorithm starts

2. Condition number: runtime scales as kappa^2
   -> ill-conditioned (real-world) systems erase the gain

3. Readout: |x> -> one classical number costs measurement
   -> reading the WHOLE vector costs at least O(N)
caption: Put all three together and the speedup is real only in a narrow regime — not "any" system, not unconditionally "exponential."

steps.label: Popular coverage quotes log(N) and drops all three caveats
steps.sub: That's exactly the reputation this lesson is correcting

steps.label: Not fake, not useless — genuinely exponential when conditions hold
steps.sub: Efficient state prep, small κ, and a single aggregate readout

steps.label: State the precondition, not just the exponent
A pattern you'll see again and again in this course
steps.sub: Every real speedup claim comes with a scope
